title: OD-MoE: On-Demand Expert Loading for Cacheless Edge-Distributed MoE Inference. Liujianfu Wang, Yuyang Du, Yuchen Pan, Soung Chang Liew, Jiacheng Liu, Kexin Chen (CUHK). arXiv:2512.03927v1 [cs.DC], 3 Dec 2025
setup: Mixtral-8x7B (8 experts/layer, top-2, 32 layers), full-precision experts. Ten nodes on a 1 Gbps Ethernet LAN: main node (1x RTX 3090, 128 GB DRAM, non-experts), shadow node (2x RTX 3090, 128 GB, INT8 copy of the whole model, 45 GB), 8 worker nodes (1x RTX 3090, 192 GB DRAM each; each worker holds <1 GB of GPU memory, experts are fetched CPU DRAM -> GPU just in time over PCIe). All nodes AMD R7-7700. Baselines run on a separate server: 8x RTX 3090, EPYC 7K62, 512 GB DRAM (Transformers needs 8 GPUs; offloaders use one GPU). Batch 1 greedy decode; HOBBIT test set: 60 Alpaca prompts, input 16 or 128 tokens, output 64 or 256. Software: PyTorch/Transformers-based; llama.cpp CPU baseline. No disk/NVMe involved: experts come from DRAM.

numbers.what: OD-MoE vs llama.cpp (CPU, all experts in DRAM)

numbers.baseline: Transformers 417 ms; Mixtral-Offloading 1845; MoE-Infinity 6119; HOBBIT 5680; AdapMoE 1387; llama.cpp 4288
numbers.ratio: 5.4x slower than Transformers; slower than Mixtral-Offloading and AdapMoE

Recall without alignment (INT8 shadow, no token/KV alignment)
numbers.value: ~100% falling to ~30% by token 256, mean ~45%; random prefetch ~25%

numbers.baseline: full model on 8 GPUs (~180 GB listed for Transformers)
Mixtral-Offloading 2.1725, MoE-Infinity 0.6675, HOBBIT 0.7575, AdapMoE 3.0350, Transformers 4.8425, llama.cpp 0.7975

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Each worker <1 GB, but the shadow node uses 45 GB and main 7 GB; total 60 GB

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: catalog one-liner: shadow model predicts experts
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: INT8/NF4/FP16 emulative shadow copy ("SEP"), aligned every iteration

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: catalog one-liner: "Reaches about 7..." (text cut off at 204 chars in the CSV)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Cannot be checked; paper reports 75.5% of the all-GPU-cached speed, 3.69 tok/s. If the cut text was "about 75%" it is right.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: 3.69 tok/s = 75.5% of 4.89; 4.49x llama.cpp 0.82; recall 99.94% FP16
first pass: HOBBIT 0.79, MoE-Infinity 0.69, AdapMoE 3.13, Mixtral-Offloading 2.24
first pass: INT8 recall collapses to ~30% by token 256 without alignment
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Text says ~30% by token 256 (mean ~45%) for the no-alignment INT8 case

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: "experts from DRAM not disk"
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Workers have 192 GB DRAM; experts loaded CPU DRAM -> GPU

why: Assumes GPU nodes (RTX 3090 each), batch 1 but 8 experts/layer with top-2 so one expert fits one worker; experts sit in 128-192 GB DRAM per node, never on disk; the LAN carries only activations (16 KB/token/layer) and alignment KV (256 KB/token). The predictor needs a second INT8 copy of the whole model on a 2-GPU node plus per-token alignment traffic, impossible on an 8-32 GB CPU machine; with 512 experts, top-10 the "one expert per worker" parallelism does not apply. The baseline llama.cpp number (0.82) is a CPU run on another server with all experts resident, so 4.49x is a GPU-vs-CPU gap, not a method gain.
quality_loss: None for OD-MoE itself (full-precision experts; Table 2(iii) shows it matches Transformers/llama.cpp on six benchmark groups). Quantised offloading baselines lose quality (their benchmark rows drop, e.g. BigBenchHard and Big Code in Table 2(iii)).
ablation: Yes, Fig 8 (six cases: shadow node with/without token and KV alignment, random prefetch, load-after-routing) and Fig 9/10 (alignment periods). Token alignment matters more than KV alignment; without the shadow model the speed falls to the I/O-bound regime. No cache-vs-prefetch ablation because there is no cache.
limitations: Authors state: predictor accuracy decays unless aligned; alignment trades accuracy against cost; best period depends on GPU (RTX 3080 optimum differs). They do not discuss disk, non-8-expert models, or batch>1 (decoding is batch 1 only).
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction. Its high-recall predictor (99.9%) needs a shadow model; our measured predictor precision (0.55) is a cheap-predictor figure and OD-MoE itself shows recall ~25-45% when the shadow is not aligned, consistent with cheap predictors being weak. pubtech E.md wording "about 75% of a GPU-cached Mixtral speed" is correct.

title: Accelerating Edge Inference for Distributed MoE Models with Latency-Optimized Expert Placement ("Prism" in v4). Tian Wu, Liming Wang, Zijian Wen, Xiaoxi Zhang, Xu Chen, Jingpu Duan, Xianwei Zhang, Jinhang Zuo (SYSU, CityU HK, Peng Cheng Lab). arXiv:2508.12851v4 [cs.DC], 15 Apr 2026
id_read: arXiv 2508.12851 latest (v4) PDF, full text. A search-result snippet shows the v1 abstract page titled the system "DanceMoE"; v1 not read.
setup: Testbed is ONE machine: 4x A100-40GB, 256 GB RAM, split into 3 simulated edge servers (1, 1, 2 GPUs) joined by a Docker network limited to 500 Mbps with tc. Models: Mixtral-8x7B (32 layers, top-2 of 8) and DeepSeek-V2-Lite (26 layers, top-8 of 64); GPU memory artificially capped to 70% (Mixtral) / 30% (DeepSeek). Datasets BIG-bench, MMLU-Pro, WikiText, TACO; output length 20 tokens or answer length; requests arrive as Poisson (10 s / 20 s mean inter-arrival). Baselines: Uniform, Redundance (own heuristic), SmartMoE placement module, EPLB (re-implemented by the authors for heterogeneity). Migration every 5 min. Plus an event-driven simulator for 4-256 GPUs and 100-1000 Mbps.

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Placement is activation-aware and entropy-driven to maximise local compute ratio under memory limits, plus runtime migration; it is about request locality across heterogeneous servers, not hop count

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Table II is serve latency under Poisson arrivals and includes queueing (values up to 48 s), not per-token decode latency

why: Multi-user serving across 3 GPU "servers" with queueing; experts live in GPU memory partitions, no disk; placement uses per-server request distributions (input locality across servers) which does not exist for one user on one laptop. Edge testbed is a single 4-GPU box with throttled network.
ablation: Migration on/off (Fig 7), baselines Uniform/Redundance/SmartMoE/EPLB; no isolation of cache vs layout vs prefetch.
limitations: Gains shrink with few experts (Mixtral ~2-3%); depends on workload locality; heterogeneity assumptions; edge environment simulated.
contradicts_our_findings: No. Its small Mixtral gain (2-3%) and our held-out balanced split (1.266 -> 1.250 straggler) both say placement refinements recover little when routing is near uniform.

title: Exploiting Inter-Layer Expert Affinity for Accelerating Mixture-of-Experts Model Inference (ExFlow). Jinghan Yao, Quentin Anthony, Aamir Shafi, Hari Subramoni, Dhabaleswar K. Panda (Ohio State). arXiv:2401.08383v2 [cs.LG], 17 Jan 2024 (IEEE conference style; venue not printed in the text)
setup: GPT-style MoE models, top-1 gating: GPT-M 350M with 8/16/32/64 experts per layer (24 layers), also 32/40-layer variants and a GPT-XL (1.3B, 16 experts). Hardware: Wilkes3 cluster, nodes with 2x AMD EPYC 7763 and 4x A100-80GB (NVLink), dual-rail HDR200 InfiniBand; 1-8 nodes (4-32+ GPUs). Baseline: DeepSpeed-MoE expert parallelism (two Alltoalls per layer). Method: context-coherent expert parallelism (one Alltoall instead of two) plus an integer program for expert-to-GPU placement from routing traces on Pile (a few thousand tokens suffice); evaluated on Pile eval, affinity re-tested on C4, Dolma, Yelp (Table III).

numbers.value: placement solved on Pile gives almost identical affinity on C4/Dolma/Yelp (normalised ~0.99-1.00)

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: The method has two parts: single-Alltoall context-coherent EP AND affinity placement; most of the gain at 2.2x needs both

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: up to 2.2x throughput and up to 67% lower routing latency
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: matches abstract; 2.2x is the best single configuration (MoE-16, 2 experts/GPU)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: Alltoall ~15% on 1 node, 63% on 2, 76% on 8
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: as above

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: "GPT MoE 350M-1.3B top-1, A100 NVLink+IB"
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Table II models 350M/470M/590M/1.3B, top-1 at inference

why: Gain is communication volume between GPUs in expert parallelism for batched serving; top-1 gating; tiny models. In our regime (one node pair at best, batch 1, top-10 of 512, bandwidth bound by NVMe) there is no Alltoall to remove. Useful signal: inter-layer routing conditional probabilities are strongly peaked and stable across datasets (Table III) - supports next-layer expert prediction for prefetch, which is the part that could transfer.
ablation: ExFlow with vs without affinity placement (Fig 10: "ExFlow w/o affinity" vs "w. affinity") separates the single-Alltoall change from the placement; I did not extract the per-bar numbers (bar chart), so the size of the placement-only share is not quantified here.
limitations: Requires pre-trained model profile (1000-3000 tokens); gain shrinks when each GPU holds one expert per layer or on 4 GPUs of one node (NVLink Alltoall cheap); trains on GPT-style top-1 only.
contradicts_our_findings: Consistent: our held-out balanced split gained little (1.266 -> 1.250). Affinity helps when whole Alltoall volume is the cost; with top-10 of 512 per token and two nodes the straggler dominates, not communication.

why: FlashMoE is the closest single-machine NVMe expert-streaming paper: same expert-granular files, batch 1, ~3 ms per expert read, RAM squeezed to 1 GB free. But the expert cache is in 16 GB of VRAM (9-38% of experts per layer), compute on GPU, and Qwen3-30B has 128 experts (not 512). Its relevant message is that cache policy beats LRU by 7-22% decode (hit rate 73% LRU vs 86% Belady) at equal cache. MoE-SpeQ/Specter needs a GPU, a quantised draft model resident on device, speculative multi-token verification (batch>1 verification) and host DRAM; none is available CPU-only in 8-32 GB.
quality_loss: FlashMoE: none (exact). MoE-SpeQ/Specter: lossless w.r.t. the target (INT4 draft, FP16 target verifies); speed falls with draft accuracy.
ablation: FlashMoE: policy comparison LRU/LFU/ARC/LeCaR/ML at several cache sizes (Fig 6, 7b,e) isolates the replacement policy; no prefetch ablation. Specter: Table 5b (PIO/SIC/SEE) and Table 6 isolate prefetch accuracy.
limitations: FlashMoE: policy trained offline on TriviaQA traces; no stated limitations section; routing-trace generalisation to other domains not tested. Specter: depends on draft quality; A100 only.
contradicts_our_findings: Mild: FlashMoE shows LRU is 13 points below Belady in hit rate (73% vs 86%), so our "LRU already hits 0.567 at 8 GB" best path is not at the policy ceiling; a learned recency+frequency policy might add 7-22% decode speed. Their gain is relative to LRU, so it does not contradict our numbers but is a missed lever in our simulations. Also their SSD read 3 ms/expert vs our 2.7 MB reads at 3.1 GB/s is consistent.

title: Training-Free Activation Sparsity in Large Language Models (TEAL). James Liu, Pragaash Ponnusamy, Tianle Cai, Han Guo, Yoon Kim, Ben Athiwaratkun (MIT, Together AI, Princeton). "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025", arXiv:2408.14690v3, 25 Feb 2025
setup: Dense models only: Llama-2 7B/13B/70B, Llama-3 8B/70B, Mistral-7B. Magnitude thresholding of the inputs to every linear layer (calibrated per layer, greedy per-layer sparsity). Speed: GPT-Fast with CUDA graphs + torch.compile, FP16, batch 1, ~5 input tokens, up to 200 output tokens, A6000 (300 W) and A100 (500 W); Llama-3-70B uses tensor parallel (TP2 A100, TP4 A6000). Custom sparse GEMV kernel. LM head not sparsified. Quantisation compatibility only shown as perplexity (Fig 4: 8-bit RTN, 4-bit AWQ, 2/3-bit QuIP#); quantised-sparse speed explicitly left to future work. No MoE experiments.

why: Real batch-1 speedups, but from a GPU memory-bound dense FP16 GEMV with CUDA graphs: skipping weight columns for zeroed activations. In our regime (4.3-bit experts streamed from NVMe at 3 GB/s) the saving only materialises if unneeded weight columns are not read from disk, which needs column-contiguous (strided) layout and small reads; the gate/up inputs are the same for every row so the sparsity pattern is per token, and the union over a draft/prefetch window fills in. Speed with quantisation is NOT measured. Batch scaling is poor (paper: Wdown sparsity at 50% model-wide drops from ~60% at batch 1 to ~38% at batch 4). MoE: the paper only speculates that MoE low-batch is "less difficult"; no results.
quality_loss: Table 1-2: Llama-3-8B +0.34 ppl and -1.86 downstream points at 40%; +0.80 ppl and -4.65 points at 50%; larger models (70B) lose 1.1-2.2 points. 65% degrades significantly.
ablation: Yes: per-layer greedy allocation vs uniform, input sparsity vs output sparsity for Wup (Sec 5.4.1), prefill sparsification (Sec 5.4.3), batch size (Sec 5.4.4). No ablation on memory-transfer (disk) vs compute.
limitations: Authors: does not scale to higher batch sizes; LM head not sparsified; sparse+quantised kernels left to future work; MoE note is speculation.
contradicts_our_findings: No. Their 1.5-1.8x ceiling equals our closed-form gate-first byte gain at d=0.5 (1.50x) and TEAL is the dense case without our expert-union and 57% dense-compute limits. Our reading in E.md (family 12) is consistent; note the 1.53x/1.8x are the best two entries of Table 3, not a typical value (1.25-1.63x).
